program: Travel English -- Europe Without a Translator
hub_subtitle: Travel English for the airport, the check-in counter, the hotel and passport control — so that Europe needs no translator

lesson.menu_title: Rosângela's Final Rehearsal -- Gate to Hotel Door
lesson.menu_desc: The next trip is booked, and tonight is the dress rehearsal: the gate, the shuttle, the street, the front desk — with nobody to translate and nothing written down. The tool of the evening is the politest one in English: the indirect question, the frame you use when you have to ask a stranger and you want a real answer. The grammar: Could you tell me where the shuttle stops?, Do you know if this bus goes downtown?, I was wondering if you could help me — no inversion after the question word, and if for a yes-or-no question. New words for finding your way: directions, straight ahead, around the corner, a shuttle, on foot, to get lost, a backup plan, just in case, to head to, confident -- 36 slides

lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosângela | Lesson 19 -- Rosângela's Final Rehearsal
lesson.grammar_point: indirect questions (Could you tell me where...? / Do you know if...? / I was wondering if...) -- no inversion in the second part, and if for yes-no questions

listenings.text: My name is Martin, and I stand behind an information desk in a European airport, eleven hours a day, and I answer questions. Thousands of them. So let me tell you something that nobody tells travelers, and that costs nothing to learn. It is not your grammar that decides the answer you get from me. It is the first four words of your question. When somebody walks up and says, where is the shuttle, flat, like that, I answer in five seconds and I look at the next person. When somebody says, excuse me, could you tell me where the shuttle stops, I stop, I look up, and I tell them the stop, and the time, and that the second one is closer to their hotel, and that on Sunday it only runs every forty minutes. Same information desk. Same man. Same day. Two completely different answers. And here is the part that surprises people. Those four words are not about being polite for the sake of being polite. They are about time. Excuse me, could you tell me gives me one second to turn my head, and it tells me you are going to ask something real. I hear people with beautiful English get short answers, and I hear people with fifty words of English get my whole attention, because they opened the door before they walked through it. So if you are nervous about your English, do not spend the night before your trip studying verbs. Learn four openings by heart. Excuse me, could you tell me. Do you know if. Sorry to bother you. I was wondering if you could help me. Say them in the mirror until they come out without thinking, and every stranger in Europe becomes a person who wants to help you.

I am Teresa, I am sixty-nine, and I want to tell you about the strangest evening of my life. Two weeks before my first trip alone, I sat down in my kitchen in the evening and I did the whole journey out loud, in English, to nobody. My daughter thought I had lost my mind. I started at the gate. I said, excuse me, could you tell me if this is the gate for the two o'clock flight. Then I stood up, I walked to the door, and I was in the arrivals hall. I said, do you know where I can find a shuttle to the center. Then the street. Do you know if the hotel is far, can I go on foot. Then the front desk. Good evening, I have a reservation under Teresa. And I did it again the next night, and the night after that, until the sentences came out of my mouth by themselves, the way your telephone number does. It took forty minutes each time. Now, listen, because this is the part that matters. Three weeks later I was standing in a real airport, at ten at night, and the shuttle was not where the paper said it was. And I did not freeze. My mouth opened and the sentence came out, already made: excuse me, could you tell me where the shuttle stops now. A woman pointed around the corner, and I was at my hotel in twenty minutes. I did not need more English that night. I needed the sentences to be ready before I was scared. That is what a rehearsal is. You are not learning the words. You are putting them somewhere you can reach them with your hands shaking.

structure.title: Four openings that turn a stranger into somebody who helps you
cards: Could you tell me + where / what time / how

This is the frame you will use most. After "could you tell me", the question goes back to normal order: subject first, verb second. "Could you tell me where the shuttle stops?" "Could you tell me what time the last train leaves?" "Could you tell me how I get to the center?" Notice what does NOT happen: no "where IS the shuttle", no "what time DOES it leave". The question word does its job, and then the sentence relaxes.
Do you know if + subject + verb

When your question has no question word and the answer is yes or no, you need the little word "if". "Do you know if this bus goes downtown?" "Do you know if the hotel is far?" "Do you know if the shuttle runs on Sunday?" Never "do you know does this bus go" and never "do you know is the hotel far": the "if" replaces all of that, and the verb stays plain.
I was wondering if you could...

Use this when you are asking for a favor and not for information: "I was wondering if you could help me." "I was wondering if you could write the address down for me." It sounds long, and that length is exactly the point: it gives the other person a second to decide to help you, and almost nobody says no to it.
Excuse me / Sorry to bother you
the four words that buy you the answer

These come BEFORE everything else, and they are not decoration. They make the other person stop and look up. "Excuse me, could you tell me where the taxis are?" "Sorry to bother you, do you know if this is the right platform?" A short question with no opening gets a short answer. The same question with an opening gets the answer, plus the thing you did not know to ask about.

items.situation: You are at the airport and you cannot find your gate on the screen. Ask a member of the ground staff.
tips: Excuse me, could you tell me where gate twenty-two is?
Sorry to bother you, do you know which gate the flight to Lisbon leaves from?

items.situation: You want to be sure the flight is still leaving at the time on your ticket. Ask.
tips: Could you tell me if the flight is still on time?
Do you know if there is a delay?

items.situation: You have landed, you have your bag, and you need the shuttle to the city. Ask somebody at the information desk.
tips: Excuse me, could you tell me where the shuttle stops?
Do you know if there is a shuttle to the center from here?

items.situation: It is late and you want to know how often the shuttle runs. Ask.
tips: Could you tell me how often the shuttle runs at this time?
Do you know what time the last shuttle leaves?

items.situation: You are in the street with your suitcase and you want to know if you can walk to the hotel. Ask somebody.
tips: Excuse me, do you know if the hotel is far? Can I go on foot?
Could you tell me if it is walking distance from here?

items.situation: The street names are not helping and you are not sure where you are anymore. Ask for help, and be soft about it.
tips: Sorry to bother you, I think I am lost. Could you tell me where this street is on the map?
I was wondering if you could help me. I am looking for this address.

items.situation: You want the person to write the address down for you, because you will not remember it.
tips: I was wondering if you could write it down for me.
Could you write the address here, please? I do not want to get lost.

items.situation: You are at the front desk at last, and you want to know what time you can have breakfast in the morning.
tips: Could you tell me what time breakfast starts?
Do you know if breakfast is included?
